strengths: The paper contributes an original and practically useful approach to a difficult geometric estimation problem. Centroid-based virtual correspondences enable four-point, three-view pose estimation through established 5-point/6-point and P3P solvers. Refinement on the original observations makes the calibrated formulation particularly compelling.

Table 2 demonstrates meaningful practical gains. On PhotoTourism, 4p3v(M)+R+F achieves AUC@10 of 69.06 at 30.54 ms, versus 66.63 at 76.45 ms for the HC baseline. The shifted, refined, filtered variant nearly matches 5pt+P3P accuracy (70.47 versus 70.54) while reducing runtime from 105.50 to 75.78 ms.

The evaluation is substantial: 5,000 triplets per scene, PhotoTourism and five Cambridge Landmarks scenes, two RANSAC frameworks, noise and outlier experiments, and component ablations. Hyperparameters are selected on a held-out scene. Supplementary results using the stricter error across all camera pairs strengthen the conclusions, and the time–accuracy curves support usefulness under computational constraints.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges approximation, scene dependence, and the limited benefit of learning after refinement. The geometric argument and empirical investigation of centroid correspondences provide useful insight. Standard solver components and detailed network training specifications make the approach accessible. The supported calibrated-camera contribution favors acceptance despite reservations about the secondary contributions.
weaknesses: The unknown-focal-length extension has a weaker demonstrated practical advantage. Every proposed variant in Table 3 is less accurate and slower than 6pt+P3P: the basic mean variant achieves AUC@10 of 49.88 versus 56.79, at 12.67 versus 11.72 ms. The best proposed variant reaches 53.56 but takes 259.63 ms. Using fewer correspondences remains valuable, but focal-length accuracy and time–accuracy experiments at low inlier ratios are missing for this formulation.

The geometric bound is too loose to explain reliably when the approximation succeeds: bounding epipolar error by triangle size does not establish small error or stable pose recovery. Table 1 shows substantial scene-dependent accuracy losses, and the manuscript acknowledges difficulty with small overlap. The broad empirical results establish usefulness on the tested data, but the operating limits under depth variation, perspective distortion, and poorly conditioned samples remain insufficiently characterized.

The learned component provides little demonstrated benefit after refinement while adding substantial cost. On PhotoTourism, L+R obtains AUC@10 of 69.88 at 297.88 ms, compared with 69.90 at 74.94 ms for M+R. There is also a technical ambiguity: Equation (2) gives a signed residual as the training loss, without an absolute value or square. As written, minimizing it does not minimize distance to the epipolar line; the actual implemented objective is unclear.

Reproducibility and reporting need clarification. Numeric RANSAC inlier thresholds, refinement parameterization, and the RANSAC adaptation described in Section 9.7 are unspecified, while code release is only promised. Table 9 reports identical accuracies and nearly identical runtimes for corresponding M±δ and L±δ variants despite their differing solver costs in Table 10. These issues particularly weaken confidence in the secondary comparisons, although they do not overturn the main calibrated-camera evidence.
